newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIAN FORWARD DOLLAR PREMIUMS RISE ON RBI MOVE.
newsitem.headline: INDIAN FORWARD DOLLAR PREMIUMS RISE ON RBI MOVE.

text.p: Indian forward dollar premiums opened up on Tuesday following a Reserve Bank of India (RBI) decision to allow foreign funds to hedge their investment in Indian debt, foreign exchange dealers said on Tuesday.
July dollars opened at 1.67 rupees against the previous close of 1.59 rupees, a foreign bank dealer said.
"Premiums are up by about four paise across the board," he said, attributing it to Monday's RBI announcement.
The RBI on Monday said authorised foreign exchange dealers are now allowed to provide forward cover to foreign institutional investors (FIIs) for their Indian debt investments.
"The extent of the cover would be limited to the current value of the investments in debt instruments translated in dollar terms," the central bank said in a statement.
Sunil Sharma, chief forex dealer at ANZ Grindlays Bank, said actual FII investment in debt would be at $100-$150 million.
"Given the steady rupee, you won't expect all of them to be covered," Sharma said. "I would think it is reasonable to expect hedging of about 25 percent of this amount."
The rupee has been stable, between 35.70 and 35.85 over the last year.
FIIs were allowed to invest in Indian debt earlier this year and leading European and American investment banks have committed over $2.0 billion funds for Indian debt.
But few funds have actively begun investing because of several problems, including the unavailability of forward cover.
Some foreign funds welcomed the RBI decision.
An FII spokesman said his firm was looking forward to a detailed circular from the central bank.
RBI announced forward cover only for debt investments, triggering speculation whether the same was in store for equity investments at a later stage.
Cumulative FII investments in Indian equities exceed $6.0 billion.
"I think they are testing the waters in debt, where the volumes are smaller," said a dealer at a French bank.
"My own personal view, looking at the way India likes to liberalise, is that this is the first step to relaxation (permission to hedge) in equities also," said ANZ's Sharma.
